node.responsibility: Establish that a whole (e.g., a strip, square, or set of objects) must be divided into parts of equal size or quantity for fraction language to apply, and distinguish equal partitions from unequal ones.
node.academicBoundary: Limit to visual and physical partitioning of a single whole into 2, 3, 4, or 6 equal parts using shapes such as strips, squares, or circles distinct from the worksheet's rectangle/circle examples (e.g., a hexagon, a number line segment, or a set of counters). Do not yet introduce fraction notation or naming; focus only on the concept of 'equal-sized parts.' No comparison across wholes.
node.evidenceGoal: Student can correctly identify which of several partitioned shapes/sets show equal parts versus unequal parts, and can partition a new whole into a specified number of equal parts.

artifact.title: The Fair-Split Guild
artifact.audienceRationale: Reina's data shows near-perfect completion and very high engagement (0.99) on precise, self-checking, high-repetition tasks (spell-check) and strong tolerance for grinding through many trials even at moderate accuracy (word-radar: 112 plays, 0.66 accuracy, engagement 0.86 despite frustration 0.27). She likes performance-flavored formats (wheel-of-fortune, pronunciation) but with low confidence/low volume, suggesting she prefers items she can practice repeatedly and master rather than one-shot spectacle. This node is built as a high-volume, instantly-checkable 'inspection and fixing' loop: many quick rounds, crisp right/wrong feedback, no reading-heavy notation yet, and a satisfying visual 'snap to equal' correction — mirroring the precision-and-repetition pattern she already thrives on, while keeping frustration low with forgiving retry mechanics.
artifact.openingPromise: You'll become the Guild's Fair-Split Inspector — the only judge who can tell a truly equal split from a sneaky uneven one, and fix the bad ones with your own hands.
artifact.firstThreeSeconds: A hexagon-shaped cookie tray appears on a workbench, already sliced into 6 pieces — two of them obviously bigger than the rest. A stamp icon glows over it, inviting a tap: 'FAIR' or 'UNFAIR'.
artifact.firstAction: Tap the stamp that matches what you see: FAIR (all pieces same size) or UNFAIR (pieces are different sizes) — no reading required, just looking and tapping.
artifact.interactionDemonstration: The first tray is deliberately obvious: two huge slices and four tiny slivers. As soon as Reina taps 'UNFAIR', the unequal lines pulse red, then a helper hand redraws them into 6 identical wedges while a chime plays, showing exactly what 'fair' looks like before she's asked to judge anything harder.
artifact.coreInteraction: Across many quick rounds, Reina inspects a whole (hexagon tray, number-line ribbon, or a scattered set of counters split into groups) and (1) stamps it FAIR or UNFAIR, then (2) if UNFAIR, drags slice-boundaries or regroups counters until a live 'equalness meter' locks green at perfectly equal — and separately, on 'Build' rounds, she's given a whole and a target part-count (2, 3, 4, or 6) and must partition it herself from scratch until the meter locks green. Every action gets instant visual feedback with no penalty for retrying.
artifact.mathAsPower: Being able to instantly spot 'equal vs. not equal' is the secret power that makes fraction language possible at all — Reina becomes the one person in the Guild who can certify any split as fair, which is the exact gatekeeping skill needed before anyone can even say 'a third' or 'a sixth' truthfully.
artifact.stakes: Guild customers (a baker, a ribbon-maker, a marble-collector) are waiting for their orders to be certified. An uncorrected unequal split gets shipped out with a wobbly, sad customer reaction; a properly fixed one gets a happy stamp of approval and the order ships with a cheer.
artifact.consequences: Misjudging FAIR/UNFAIR causes the tray to visibly wobble and tip over (pieces sliding off), giving immediate honest feedback without harsh punishment — she simply gets to look again and re-stamp. Successfully corrected splits get sealed with a wax Guild stamp and added to a growing 'certified orders' shelf.
artifact.recovery: No lives, no timers. Wrong stamps or clumsy drags just trigger a gentle 'wobble and reset' animation with a soft sound, and the piece returns to its editable state so she can keep adjusting the equalness meter until it locks green — unlimited attempts, always forward progress once corrected.
progression: Warm-up: obvious FAIR vs UNFAIR judgments on hexagons and strips (2 and 4 parts), heavy visual contrast
Judge + Fix: subtler unequal splits (near-equal but not quite) requiring drag-to-adjust corrections, introducing 3 and 6 parts
Sets of objects: counters grouped unevenly (e.g., 7 marbles in groups of 4 and 3) vs evenly (6 marbles in groups of 3 and 3), extending 'equal' beyond shapes to quantities
Build-from-scratch: given a blank whole and a target number of parts (2, 3, 4, or 6), partition it herself with no starting shape to judge, only the equalness meter as a guide
Mixed mastery round: a rapid shuffle of judge, fix, and build tasks across strips, number lines, hexagons, and counter sets, timed only as an optional personal-best challenge
artifact.worldReaction: The workbench fills up with a shelf of stamped, certified orders; customer characters visibly cheer, do a little dance, or offer thank-you notes when their split is fixed, while the Guildmaster's portrait in the background nods approvingly and adds new tools (a laser-straight ruler, a counter-sorting tray) to Reina's bench as she progresses.
artifact.payoff: Reina earns the title 'Certified Fair-Split Inspector' and unlocks a golden stamp tool plus a display case showing every whole she's successfully equalized, from hexagons to ribbon number-lines to marble jars — visible proof of a skill fully mastered before any fraction names are even introduced.
artifact.replayVariation: Randomized whole-shapes (hexagon, strip, circle-of-counters, number line, irregular blob), randomized part-counts (2, 3, 4, 6), randomized near-miss unequal splits of varying subtlety, and an optional speed-run mode for repeat play once accuracy is consistently high.
artifact.visualDirection: Warm, tactile workshop aesthetic — wood-grain workbench, chalky stamps, hand-drawn-style trays and ribbons; equal parts glow soft green, unequal parts pulse warm red/orange; the 'equalness meter' is a simple horizontal gauge that fills and locks with a golden glow.
artifact.motionDirection: Snappy, satisfying micro-animations: slices slide and snap into place with slight overshoot-and-settle physics; unequal pieces visibly wobble/tilt to show imbalance; the wax stamp comes down with a quick squash-and-bounce.
artifact.soundDirection: Light, tactile sound design — soft wood-clink for taps, a rising chime as the equalness meter fills, a satisfying 'thunk' wax-stamp sound on certification, gentle low 'wobble' thud for mistakes, upbeat short jingle on level completion.
usefulLibraries: Phaser (2D interaction, drag physics, tweening for snap/wobble effects)
Matter.js or Phaser Arcade Physics (optional wobble/tip physics on unequal trays)
artifact.engagementPrediction: High: matches Reina's demonstrated preference for high-repetition, instantly-checkable tasks with clear visual right/wrong feedback and low reading load; forgiving retry loop should keep frustration low (similar to her low-frustration spell-check pattern) while volume of quick rounds mirrors her word-radar stamina.
artifact.falsifyingEvidence: If Reina's completion rate drops sharply on Build-from-scratch rounds (self-directed partitioning) compared to Judge/Fix rounds, or if she disengages after few plays despite instant feedback, it would suggest she needs more structured scaffolding before open-ended partitioning, contradicting the assumption that she can transfer inspection skill directly into construction skill.

node.responsibility: Connect equally partitioned wholes to unit fraction names and notation (1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5), recognizing that a unit fraction represents one equal part out of the total number of equal parts.
node.academicBoundary: Use fresh contexts (e.g., a triangle divided into thirds, a set of 8 apples divided into fourths, a number line marked in halves) rather than the worksheet's rectangle and circle. Restrict to unit fractions only (numerator of 1); do not introduce non-unit fractions (e.g., 2/3) or fraction comparison.
node.evidenceGoal: Student can correctly name the unit fraction represented by a shaded equal part, correctly shade a specified unit fraction of a new whole, and correctly match unit fraction notation to its verbal name (e.g., '1/5' to 'one fifth').

artifact.title: The Lantern Keeper's Naming Glass
artifact.audienceRationale: Reina's evidence shows enormous volume and total completion on a scanning/detection task (word-radar, 112 plays, 0.86 engagement) and on a precision-verification task (spell-check, 167 plays, accuracy 1.00, engagement 0.99). Both are short-loop, 'find it / confirm it exactly right' formats she returns to repeatedly. Her lower accuracy in the scanning task alongside high engagement suggests she tolerates being wrong when the loop is fast and restartable, while her perfect accuracy in the verification task suggests she takes real pride in producing an exactly correct label. This design therefore pairs a scanning beat (sweep the Naming Glass across lantern panes to find the one glowing part) with a labeling beat (write the exact fraction name on the pane). Fractions notation is treated as spelling-with-meaning: 1 part out of how many. The wheel/pronunciation activities had only low-confidence positive signal, so no chance-spinning or speech input is used as a load-bearing mechanic.
artifact.openingPromise: Every lantern in the harbor has forgotten its name. You hold the only glass that can read them — and you write the names back on by hand.
artifact.firstThreeSeconds: A dark harbor. One triangular lantern hangs at center, split into three equal glass panes; one pane is glowing amber. A brass hand-glass drifts under the player's cursor with a soft hum, and a blank name-plate flickers beneath the lantern.
artifact.firstAction: Drag the brass glass over the glowing pane. The glass snaps to it, the pane brightens, and the whole lantern outlines itself while a counter under the glass ticks: 'parts: 1 … 2 … 3'. Nothing else is required yet — the count happens because you looked.
artifact.interactionDemonstration: After the glass counts 3 parts, the name-plate splits into two empty slots stacked over a bar. A ghost-hand demo types '1' on top ('the one pane you're holding') and '3' below ('the panes in the whole lantern'), then the plate speaks-in-text 'one third' and the lantern lights fully. The demo then dims and a second lantern arrives with empty slots — no ghost-hand, player's turn.
artifact.coreInteraction: Each round: (1) SWEEP — move the Naming Glass across a lantern whose whole is divided into 2, 3, 4, or 5 equal parts, until it locks onto the single glowing part; the glass audibly counts the total parts as it sweeps the whole. (2) NAME — type or tap-select the top number and bottom number on the name-plate (top is always the one part you're holding, bottom is the total). (3) SPEAK-THE-PLATE — drag the finished plate to one of three word-ribbons floating in the fog ('one fourth', 'one half', 'one fifth') to bolt the notation to its verbal name. A fourth variant round flips the job: the plate arrives already engraved (e.g., '1/5') and the lantern is dark with 5 blank equal panes — the player must ignite exactly one pane to match the engraving. Only unit fractions ever appear; the top slot is fixed at 1 and shown as pre-etched brass in early stages, unlocked for typing later.
artifact.mathAsPower: The glass cannot invent a name — it can only count. The only way to light a lantern is to state how many equal parts the whole holds and that you are holding exactly one of them. Knowing that the bottom number is the count of equal parts, not the count of glowing parts, is literally the power that turns the harbor's lights back on; guessing a bigger bottom number makes the lantern flicker and stay dark because the glass reports a mismatch in part count.
artifact.stakes: A night ferry is crossing the harbor and steers by named lanterns. A soft progress ribbon at the top shows how much of the channel is lit. Unlit lanterns leave dark gaps the ferry must slow through — the ferry never sinks, but it arrives late and the harbor stays gloomy, so the pressure is warmth and completeness rather than failure.
artifact.consequences: A correct plate: the pane's amber floods the whole lantern's frame, the name is engraved permanently, and a wedge of channel water lights up. A wrong bottom number: the lantern flickers twice and the glass overlays translucent tick-marks on every pane, whispering the real count ('I counted 4'); the plate returns blank. A wrong word-ribbon match: the ribbon slips off and re-floats with its syllables briefly separated ('one — fourth'). No lives, no timers, no score loss — only lit versus not-yet-lit.
artifact.recovery: Any lantern can be re-swept unlimited times, and holding the glass still for two seconds triggers 'slow count', which walks a bright pulse across each equal part one at a time while a number rises. After two misses on the same lantern, the whole is temporarily unfolded into a straight strip of its equal parts so the count is trivially visible, then folded back for the naming step. A 'Relight' button on any dark lantern in the finished harbor returns the player to that exact puzzle without disturbing lit ones.
progression: Stage 1 — Triangle Lanterns: three-pane and two-pane triangular lanterns. Top slot pre-etched '1'. Player types only the bottom number. Introduces 1/3 and 1/2.
Stage 2 — Hex and Strip Lanterns: hexagonal lanterns in halves and thirds, plus long lamp-strips divided into fourths and fifths. Bottom number typed; word-ribbon matching begins with two choices.

Stage 3 — Basket Lanterns (sets): a hanging basket of 8 glow-fruit split into 4 equal bunches of 2, or 10 shells split into 5 equal groups — one bunch glowing. Player names 1/4 or 1/5 of a set, learning the whole can be a collection.

Stage 4 — Reverse Ignition: the plate is pre-engraved (1/5, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2) on a dark, blank, equally-divided whole; player must ignite exactly one part. Wrong count of ignited parts is refused gently ('the plate says one').

Stage 5 — Mile-Marker Lanterns: a number-line rope from 0 to 1 with lamp-posts at every equal step (halves, thirds, fourths, fifths). Player names the single step-length being held, then drags the plate to the correct post label.

Stage 6 — Keeper's Round: mixed shapes, sets, and rope-lines, both plate-writing and word-ribbon matching, top slot now blank and typed by the player, three lanterns lit in a row to finish the channel.
artifact.worldReaction: The harbor answers rather than praises. Named lanterns hum a note whose pitch matches the denominator family, so a lit stretch becomes a small chord. Fog retreats from lit water. Gulls settle on named lanterns and take off from dark ones. The ferry's bell sounds once each time a channel wedge completes, and its silhouette visibly speeds up. At stage transitions the Lantern Keeper's silhouette on the pier hands over a heavier, brighter glass.
artifact.payoff: The ferry glides the full channel and its passengers' lanterns answer the harbor's chord. The camera pulls back to a 'Naming Ledger' — a page where every lantern the player named appears as a tiny shape with its notation and word beside it (1/2 one half, 1/3 one third, 1/4 one fourth, 1/5 one fifth), sorted by denominator. The player is given the Keeper's title and one blank lantern to name and keep, which appears in the harbor on every future visit.
artifact.replayVariation: The harbor regenerates each night: lantern shapes are drawn from a pool (triangle, hexagon, trapezoid, lamp-strip, fruit basket, shell tray, rope-line), the glowing part's position within the whole is randomized, denominators are shuffled across 2/3/4/5, and each night has one 'featured' denominator that appears more often. Two named night modes: 'Fog Night' hides all but the pane under the glass, forcing the slow-count habit; 'Ledger Night' shows only the word ('one fifth') and asks for the notation plus the ignition. Rotation of which of the three evidence acts (name-the-shaded, shade-the-named, match-notation-to-word) opens the session keeps the first minute fresh.
artifact.visualDirection: Warm ink-and-brass storybook harbor at night: deep indigo water, charcoal silhouettes, amber glass. Lanterns are flat geometric shapes with thick dark leading between panes so equal parts read instantly at a glance. The Naming Glass is a chunky brass ring with a faint counting scale etched on its rim. Name-plates are hammered copper with a crisp horizontal bar; the fraction bar is visually the same object as the lantern's leading, reinforcing 'this line means split into equal parts'. Numerals are large, high-contrast, and hand-etched in style. Sets are drawn as glow-fruit or shells in visibly identical bunches with rope dividers matching the leading style.
artifact.motionDirection: Everything slow and buoyant, like lantern-light on water. The glass has slight drag-lag and a magnetic snap to a part. Counting is a single bright pulse traveling part-to-part with a small numeral popping above each. Correct naming: amber floods outward from the held part along the leading lines, then the frame breathes once. Mistake: two soft flickers and a fade-in of tick marks — never a shake or red flash. Unfolding a whole into a strip is a smooth accordion. Water light spreads as a slow wedge, and the ferry moves in a continuous drift so progress is always visible in the periphery.
artifact.soundDirection: Harbor bed: low water lap, distant buoy, faint rigging creak. The glass hums a soft continuous tone that rises one step per part counted, so the ear learns 'four parts' as four rising steps. Naming correct: a warm glass 'ting' plus a spoken plate reading the words aloud ('one fourth') at natural pace — voice is confirmation, never required input. Mismatch: a muted wooden knock and a whispered count. Each denominator family owns a bell timbre so a lit channel plays a gentle chord. Ferry bell on channel milestones. Ledger reveal: a single sustained chime under quiet page-turns.
usefulLibraries: Pixi.js — fast 2D WebGL rendering for many glowing lantern shapes and additive light layers
GSAP — timeline control for counting pulses, accordion unfold, amber flood, and ferry drift
matter-js (light use) — buoyant sway of hanging lanterns and floating word-ribbons
Poly-Decomp / custom polygon partitioner — reliably splitting arbitrary polygons into n equal-area panes for procedural lantern generation
Howler.js — layered ambient bed plus pitch-stepped counting tones and denominator bell timbres
Web Speech API (speechSynthesis) or pre-recorded audio sprites — spoken fraction names for notation-to-word confirmation
React + Zustand — stage/lantern state, ledger persistence, and 'Relight' navigation
localForage — persist the Naming Ledger and the player's kept lantern across nights
artifact.engagementPrediction: High and repeat-driven. The sweep-and-lock beat mirrors the scanning loop she has played 112 times, and the name-plate beat mirrors the exact-answer verification loop she has played 167 times at perfect accuracy; the plate is short enough (one or two digits plus a word match) to satisfy her demonstrated appetite for producing a flawless label. Full-completion history on both high-volume activities suggests she finishes sessions, so a channel-length arc with a persistent ledger and a kept lantern should pull her into multiple nights. The gentle no-loss consequence model fits her moderate frustration tolerance.
artifact.falsifyingEvidence: Falsified if she abandons before the third lantern, or if plate errors cluster on the bottom number after slow-count help has fired twice (indicating the equal-part count itself, not the naming, is unstable — a node 1 dependency). Also falsified if she reaches high accuracy on shape lanterns but drops below 60% on set and number-line lanterns, meaning she learned 'count the leading lines' rather than 'one of n equal parts'. Behavioral falsifier: she skips the sweep entirely and types denominators by guess-and-check, which would show the glass is decoration rather than the source of the answer. Replay falsifier: fewer than two returns across a week despite completing night one.

node.responsibility: Reason about and justify which unit fraction is larger when comparing 1/3 and 1/4, using the principle that dividing a whole into more equal parts produces smaller individual parts.
node.academicBoundary: Restrict comparison strictly to the pair 1/3 and 1/4 (and may extend briefly to comparing 1/2 vs 1/5 as a parallel fresh example for reinforcement) using new whole representations (e.g., two identical bars of the same length divided differently, or two identical sets of counters) distinct from the worksheet's rectangle/circle. Do not require comparing unit fractions with unlike wholes of different sizes, and do not introduce non-unit fraction comparisons.
node.evidenceGoal: Student can correctly identify that 1/3 is larger than 1/4 and provide a valid justification (e.g., referencing that three equal parts are each larger than four equal parts of the same whole), and can apply the same reasoning to a parallel unfamiliar unit fraction pair.

artifact.title: The Chocolate Caravan: Biggest Piece Wins
artifact.audienceRationale: Reina's evidence shows high engagement with high-repetition, fast-feedback verification games (spell-check: 167 plays, 99% engagement, perfect accuracy) and tolerance for scanning/judgment tasks (word-radar). She thrives on quick, confident yes/no style decisions with instant confirmation. This design gives her rapid-fire 'which piece is bigger?' judgments with immediate visual proof, plus a justification step that keeps the math honest, wrapped in a low-frustration loop she can repeat many times.
artifact.openingPromise: You are the Fairness Judge of a traveling chocolate caravan. Two hungry travelers each claim their share is bigger. Only you can slide the pieces together, see the truth, and declare the winner.
artifact.firstThreeSeconds: Two identical golden chocolate bars appear side by side on a wooden caravan table. One snaps into 3 equal pieces, the other into 4, with a satisfying crack. A fox traveler holds up one piece from the 3-bar, a badger holds one piece from the 4-bar. A speech bubble asks: 'Whose piece is BIGGER? Drag them together to find out!'
artifact.firstAction: Drag the fox's 1/3 piece down onto a comparison tray; the badger's 1/4 piece slides in beside it automatically, aligned at the left edge. The size difference is instantly, visibly obvious.
artifact.interactionDemonstration: A ghost hand demonstrates once: it drags a piece to the tray, the two pieces align, a measuring ruler-glow highlights the length difference, and a stamp icon pulses over the larger piece saying 'Tap the bigger piece to judge!'
artifact.coreInteraction: Each round: two identical wholes (bars, licorice ropes, or rows of counters) are split live in front of Reina into 3 vs 4 equal parts. She (1) predicts which single piece is bigger by tapping a traveler, (2) drags the pieces onto the aligned comparison tray to verify, then (3) stamps a justification card choosing between statements like 'More pieces means each piece is SMALLER' vs 'More pieces means each piece is BIGGER' vs 'They are the same.' Correct prediction + correct justification = a gold Fairness Seal.
artifact.mathAsPower: The insight 'cutting the same whole into more parts makes each part smaller' becomes Reina's judicial superpower: after a few verified rounds, a 'Swift Judgment' mode lets her rule correctly BEFORE the pieces are compared, earning double seals for predicting from denominators alone (3 vs 4). The math replaces the need to measure.
artifact.stakes: Each correct verdict feeds the caravan travelers fairly and adds a wagon to the caravan. Wrong verdicts leave a traveler grumbling with the smaller piece and stall the caravan at the crossroads.
artifact.consequences: A wrong prediction isn't punished harshly: the tray comparison plays out anyway, visibly showing the 1/4 piece is smaller, and the narrator says 'Look, four cuts made skinnier pieces!' The round replays with a fresh whole so Reina re-judges with the evidence in mind.
artifact.recovery: After any miss, an 'Overlay Lens' tool appears: it stacks the 1/3 piece directly on top of the 1/4 piece with the difference striped in red. Reina then re-stamps the justification card. Two assisted successes restore full seal value.
progression: Round 1-3: Bars split into 3 vs 4; drag-and-compare with full visual verification before judging.
Round 4-6: Predict first, verify second; justification card required each time.
Round 7-8: Swift Judgment mode: rule from the numbers 1/3 vs 1/4 alone, verification shown only after the verdict.
Final Bonus Crossing: a parallel fresh dispute, 1/2 vs 1/5 over a licorice rope, judged with reasoning only, cementing 'more parts, smaller parts.'
artifact.worldReaction: Travelers cheer or grumble expressively; the caravan grows longer with each seal; a wise owl notary reads back Reina's chosen justification aloud ('More equal parts make smaller pieces, so one third is bigger!') so her reasoning is echoed by the world.
artifact.payoff: The caravan reaches Festival Town where a banner unfurls: 'Reina, Fairness Judge, ruled 1/3 > 1/4 and proved it!' Her collected seals form a badge showing two bars with the principle written beneath.
artifact.replayVariation: New whole types each playthrough (chocolate bars, licorice ropes, rows of gem counters), shuffled traveler characters, and randomized which side holds which fraction; Swift Judgment adds a timer-optional streak mode for Reina's love of rapid confident loops.
artifact.visualDirection: Warm storybook caravan palette: amber wood, chocolate browns, festival reds; flat 2D vector characters with big expressive eyes; fraction pieces rendered chunky and glossy with clear equal-partition seams; comparison tray has bold left-alignment guide line.
artifact.motionDirection: Snappy break-apart animation when wholes split; pieces glide with slight ease-out onto the tray; the larger piece gets a gentle scale-pulse when stamped; caravan wagons roll in with springy bounce on each seal earned.
artifact.soundDirection: Satisfying chocolate-snap on partitioning, soft slide-whoosh on drag, a warm stamp-thunk for verdicts, celebratory tambourine jingle for correct reasoning, gentle 'hmm?' owl hoot on misses; light folk-guitar caravan loop underneath.
artifact.engagementPrediction: High: the loop mirrors the short, verifiable, mastery-oriented cycles Reina replays obsessively (spell-check), with visual comparison scanning akin to word-radar but lower frustration since verification is always available.
artifact.falsifyingEvidence: If Reina passes the drag-compare rounds but fails Swift Judgment or picks correct verdicts with wrong justification cards more than ~30% of the time, she is reading piece sizes visually without internalizing the more-parts-smaller-pieces principle, falsifying the design's claim of conceptual mastery.
